interest: For historians of the Allied Occupation of Japan, post-WWII economic reconstruction, and early Cold War trade policy, this file offers valuable insights into the delicate balance between rehabilitating Japan's export economy and protecting domestic American industries. It provides exceptionally granular data on Japan's woolen and worsted spindle and card capacity, wartime destruction, labor and food crises, and technical blending practices with synthetic and silk wastes during acute raw material shortages. Most uniquely, the correspondence illuminates early friction over occupation procurement ethics and transparency, tracing how complaints from Boston wool merchants and congressional pressure from Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr. forced the State Department to investigate SCAP's non-competitive, exclusive purchasing contract awarded to Draper and Company for Australian and New Zealand wool.
keywords: SCAP (Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers)
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.62222, spanning April 1946 to December 1948) documents U.S. government policy, economic intelligence, and commercial controversies surrounding the revival of Japan's wool and textile manufacturing industries under the Allied Occupation. The early documents address proposals by General Douglas MacArthur to expand Japanese angora wool production to one million pounds annually, counterbalanced by domestic American wool growers seeking import bans, prompting requests for a discreet Commerce Department market study. The core of the file features a detailed March 1947 Office of Intelligence Research (OIR) report evaluating prewar wool consumption, wartime structural shifts, operational spindle and card capacity, and estimated 1947 raw wool import requirements under Far Eastern Commission textile rationing standards. Later records detail SCAP arrangements allowing private foreign suppliers to deliver raw wool on consignment in exchange for processed yarn and tops, culminating in sharp inquiries from Boston wool merchants, Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr., and the State Department regarding SCAP's controversial, sole-source appointment of Draper and Company of Boston as exclusive purchasing agent for the Japanese Board of Trade.

subfiles.about: The State Department requests the Department of Commerce conduct a confidential market study to evaluate whether the U.S. can absorb an expanded Japanese angora wool output without harming domestic producers.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Edwin M. Martin refers to discussions regarding General MacArthur's suggestion that the Japanese angora wool industry could expand to one million pounds annually if market outlets exist. Because domestic U.S. producers are advocating an embargo on Japanese angora imports, the State Department asks Commerce to investigate potential market absorption and price thresholds. The letter requests estimates on marketing up to one million pounds at prewar prices with reasonable returns to Japan. Martin emphasizes that the survey and findings should be kept confidential to minimize industry controversy.
subfiles.title: Letter from Edwin M. Martin to Murray Marker requesting U.S. Market Survey on Japanese Angora Wool
subfiles.to: Murray Marker, Office of International Trade, Department of Commerce

subfiles.about: An earlier draft of the State Department's letter requesting a Department of Commerce survey on marketing Japanese angora wool in the United States.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This draft version outlines SCAP's proposal to expand Japan's angora wool production to one million pounds per year and notes domestic American opposition seeking import bans. It requests that the Department of Commerce examine potential market capacity, prices, and economic returns to Japanese producers. It matches the final letter of April 26, 1946, except for omitting the final paragraph requesting minimal publicity.
subfiles.title: Draft Letter from Edwin M. Martin to Murray Marker on Japanese Angora Wool Market Survey
subfiles.to: Murray Marker, Office of International Trade, Department of Commerce

subfiles.about: An internal memorandum transmitting an intelligence report on Japanese woolen and worsted raw wool consumption to the Division of International Resources.
subfiles.from: Charles C. Stelle, Division of Research for Far East (DRF), Department of State
subfiles.summary: Charles C. Stelle of the Division of Research for Far East forwards a copy of OIR Report No. 3436.92 to Donald D. Kennedy in the Division of International Resources. The transmittal notes that the intelligence memorandum was prepared in response to a specific request from Miss S. Bertha Burnett of the Textile Section.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum from Charles C. Stelle to Donald D. Kennedy Forwarding OIR Report No. 3436.92
subfiles.to: Donald D. Kennedy, Division of International Resources (IR), Department of State

subfiles.about: An in-depth intelligence memorandum analyzing prewar consumption, wartime damage, operating capacity, and 1947 raw wool import needs of Japan's woolen and worsted industry.
subfiles.from: Division of Research for Far East, Office of Intelligence Research, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This comprehensive intelligence report surveys Japan's prewar raw wool imports (peaking at 260 million pounds in 1937, dominated by Australia) and assesses postwar reconstruction bottlenecks. As of December 1946, Japan had only 126,127 operable worsted spindles and 270 wool cards actively running on single 10.5-hour shifts due to severe fiber shortages, food scarcity, inflation, and priority allocation given to cotton textiles. The study details widespread blending of wool with rayon staple and waste silk, projecting that domestic raw wool stockpiles would be exhausted by mid-1947. Under Far Eastern Commission consumption allocations (FEC-079/5), producing 50 million pounds of yarn in 1947 would require approximately 200,000 scoured bales of imported wool, yielding up to 30 million pounds of woolen and worsted textiles for export.
subfiles.title: OIR Report No. 3436.92: The Consumption of Raw Wool by the Japanese Woolen and Worsted Industry
subfiles.to: Textile Section / Division of International Resources, Department of State

subfiles.about: A transmittal letter forwarding SCAP's proposed operational plan for importing raw wool into Japan to the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman transmits an enclosed policy statement outlining SCAP's program for obtaining raw wool for processing in Japanese textile mills to Donald Badger of the Far Eastern Commission. Whitman suggests that the plan be made available to the Inter-Allied Trade Board (IATB) to facilitate commercial arrangements among member nations.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to Donald Badger Transmitting SCAP Wool Import Plan

subfiles.about: A seven-point policy outline governing terms under which private foreign suppliers may deliver raw wool to Japan for processing into tops and yarn.
subfiles.from: Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State / SCAP
subfiles.summary: This policy statement specifies the conditions under which private non-Japanese firms can ship raw wool to Japan for contract processing. Raw wool is billed CIF Japan to the Japanese Government through SCAP, and suppliers must contractually agree to repurchase manufactured tops and yarn at U.S. market prices in bond. Payments are settled by offsetting raw wool invoices against finished goods, with processing by-products (moils and waste) remaining in Japan. SCAP retains authority over acceptable grades of imported wool and processing instructions transmitted to Japanese mills.
subfiles.title: Statement: Plans for Importing Raw Wool to Japan
subfiles.to: Inter-Allied Trade Board / Far Eastern Commission

subfiles.about: A letter conveying inquiries from the Boston wool trade regarding procedural and financial regulations for processing raw wool in Japan.
subfiles.from: Charles J. Shehan, Acting Chief, Agricultural Materials Branch, International Resources Division, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Charles J. Shehan reports that Mr. Kearney, representing the Boston wool trade, requested specific information on behalf of a client wishing to supply raw wool to Japan in return for tops or yarn. Kearney posed four questions regarding regulatory authority, processing rates for combing and spinning, allowable currency or clean-wool payment terms, and export restrictions. Shehan encloses the SCAP policy statement and asks the Department of Commerce to reply in writing, noting that private firms must correspond directly with SCAP in Tokyo due to limited occupation staffing.
subfiles.title: Letter from Charles J. Shehan to Wilmer Weinstein on Boston Wool Trade Inquiries
subfiles.to: Wilmer Weinstein, Textiles and Leather Division, Department of Commerce

subfiles.about: State Department reply informing Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr. that inquiries regarding Japanese wool purchasing procedures have been referred to the Department of the Army.
subfiles.from: Florence Kirlin, Special Assistant to the Counselor, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Florence Kirlin replies to Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr.'s communication of May 18 regarding letters from Max W. Schwerdt of the Eug. Schwerdt Wool Company in Boston. The inquiries concerned wool buying policies and procedures adopted by government purchasing agencies in Japan. Kirlin states that such operational matters fall under the jurisdiction of the Department of the Army and confirms that the inquiry has been transferred to that department for reply.
subfiles.title: Letter from Florence Kirlin to Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr. regarding Wool Purchasing Policies
subfiles.to: Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr., United States Senate

subfiles.about: An internal State Department transfer sheet recording the transfer of Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr.'s wool inquiry to the Department of the Army.
subfiles.from: Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr., United States Senator
subfiles.summary: This official Department of State Division of Communications and Records transfer sheet records the re-routing of correspondence from Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr., dated May 18, 1948. The correspondence, dealing with wool purchasing inquiries, was officially transferred to the Department of the Army under file reference 894.62222/5-1848.
subfiles.title: State Department Transfer Sheet for Correspondence from Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr.
subfiles.to: Department of the Army / Department of State

subfiles.about: A confidential instruction from the State Department directing the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo to investigate reports of an exclusive wool purchasing agreement with Draper and Company.
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary of State, Department of State
subfiles.summary: The Acting Secretary of State instructs the Acting Political Adviser for Japan to investigate published reports that SCAP was taking wool on consignment purchased through Draper and Company of Boston at a 2.5 percent commission. The Department requests full particulars on how Draper and Company secured this exclusive commission, whether other private commercial firms were allowed to bid, and the Political Adviser's opinion on the propriety of the arrangement.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 187 to Acting Political Adviser (Tokyo) regarding Draper and Company Wool Contract
subfiles.to: Acting Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo

subfiles.about: A confidential despatch from the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo detailing the exclusive wool purchasing contract awarded to Draper and Company by SCAP and the Japanese Board of Trade.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.summary: William J. Sebald replies to Instruction No. 187, reporting details of an October 23, 1948 contract between SCAP, the Japanese Board of Trade, and Draper and Company of Boston. Under the contract, Draper was named exclusive agent to purchase up to 19 million pounds of greasy wool (valued at £3,341,500, predominantly from Australia and New Zealand) with a guaranteed minimum of 9 million pounds. Draper receives a 2.5 percent commission on broker transactions (netting 1 percent after paying broker fees) or 1 percent when buying from dealer principals. Sebald reports that the contract was signed by R. D. Cleaves and selected solely by F. A. Williams, Chief of SCAP's Textiles Division, without competitive bids or public notice, and advises the State Department to seek further policy rationale from the Department of the Army's Civil Affairs Division.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 772 from William J. Sebald on Draper and Company Wool Purchasing Contract
